_comment: Further daina (Latvian folk-song) episodes cut from L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V, after Mannhardt's daina collections. All passages paraphrase.

title.en: Why the Moon Is Pale: The Looking-Glass of Night Water
title.zh: 月何以蒼白：夜水的鏡子

region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

texts.period: Daina recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: When his spouse reproaches the Moon for his pale colour, he answers that while she shines for man by day, he can only look at himself by night in the water — the palest of the sky's lords is also its only mirror-user.
summary.zh: 當其妻責月之蒼白，月答曰：日間汝光照世人，而我唯夜以水自照——天庭諸君中最蒼白者，亦是唯一以鏡自照者。

passages.text: In comparison with the sun the moon is a very minor figure in the dainas, and his chief importance is his connexion with her. When his spouse reproaches him for his pale colour, he replies that while she shines for man by day, he can only look at himself by night in the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

passages.text: He wears a mantle of stars, and — like the sun — is liable to be destroyed, that is, eclipsed, by dragons, serpents, and witches; the pale moon is the sky's bridegroom in exile, spending his nights at the water's edge where the reflection of his own light is the only face he has.

title.en: Saule's Housework: The Unswept Floor of Heaven
title.zh: 太陽的家務：天上未掃的地

region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

texts.period: Daina recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: The Sun dwells on a mountain — the vault of heaven — and standing in mid-sky she reproves her daughters because one had not swept the floor and the other had failed to wash the table.
summary.zh: 太陽居於山上——即天穹——立於天心之時，她責備女兒們：一個未掃地，一個未洗桌。

passages.text: She dwells on a mountain — the vault of heaven — and standing in mid-sky she reproves her daughters because one had not swept the floor, while the other had failed to wash the table. In the dainas heaven is not a throne-room but a working kitchen, and the Sun is the housewife of the day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

passages.text: The daughters she scolds are the twilights; the floor of heaven unswept is a sky full of cloud. The song is sung at the loom and the wash-tub in the Latvian farmhouses, where the same scolding is given every morning to the daughters of the house — for the daughters of Saule and the daughters of the farm are one family in the songs.

title.en: God's Sons at the Solstice: Mending the Broken Sun
title.zh: 夏至時分的神之子：修補破碎之日

region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

texts.period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: Life is not all love: after the summer solstice God's sons must band the broken solar orb; they heat the bath of dawn, mow the meadows of morning, and uproot the birch-forest of the last traces of day — then off to Germany to play games.
summary.zh: 生活非唯有愛：夏至之後，神之子須箍束破碎之日輪；燒熱黎明之浴、割平晨光之草、連根拔去白晝餘燼的樺林——而後遠赴『德意志』遊戲去了。

passages.text: Both God's sons and the daughters of the sun have their tasks to perform. In Germany — the darkening west — the morning star must prepare a coat of samite, the rich hues of dawn; God's sons must band the broken solar orb after the summer solstice; they must heat the bath of dawn; and, as the workmen of Sun and Moon or the servants of Perkunas, they are reproved for not mowing the meadows — that is, for not preparing the day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

passages.text: After uprooting the birch-forest — dissipating the last traces of day — they go to Germany to play games. The Baltic year is a piece of workmanship perpetually in need of repair: the sun cracks at midsummer, the morning must be mowed and bathed into being, and the sons of God are the repairmen of the light.

title.en: The Absent Star: Why Morning Star Leaves the Sky
title.zh: 缺席之星：晨星離天之故

region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

texts.period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: When all the other stars are visible, the morning star is absent: he has gone to woo the daughter of the sun, she hastens toward him, and they are wedded in Germany — beyond the sea, in the darkening west.
summary.zh: 眾星皆現之時，唯晨星缺席：他已去求婚日之女；她趨向他，二人成婚於『德意志』——海之外的暗沉西方。

passages.text: When all the other stars are visible, the morning star is absent: he has gone to woo the daughter of the sun. She hastens toward him, and they are wedded in Germany — beyond the sea, in the darkening west.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

passages.text: The song explains the plain fact of the sky — the morning star sets as the other stars appear — as a wedding journey: the brightest of the stars leaves the choir to meet the brightest of the daughters, and the Baltic poets, who read the sky as a farm, know exactly what such an absence means.

title.en: Lovers' Quarrels: The Broken Sword and the Fished Ring

region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

texts.period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: Of course lovers quarrel: the daughter of the sun breaks the sword of God's son — dawn outshines the morning star — and in their turn God's sons deprive her of her ring, the solar disk, at evening, till they fish it up again at dawn.
summary.zh: 戀人自然有爭執：日之女折斷神之子的劍——曙光之輝壓過晨星——神之子們亦於日暮奪其環（即日輪），至黎明又自水中釣回。

passages.text: Of course lovers occasionally quarrel: the daughter of the sun breaks the sword of God's son — for dawn surpasses the brightness of the morning star; and, in their turn, God's sons deprive her of her ring — the solar disk — at evening, though they presently fish it from the sea at dawn when it falls from her finger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

passages.text: But lovers' quarrels are love's renewal: since evening star and evening twilight, morning star and morning dawn, are inseparably associated, the quarrel ends where the day ends and begins again where the day begins. The whole mythology of the Latvian dawn is a courtship that renews itself by rule, twice a day, forever.

title.en: The Golden Cock on the Daugava: Waking the Sun's Spinner
title.zh: 道加瓦河畔金雞：喚醒太陽的紡者

region.zh: 拉脫維亞道加瓦河（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: On the edge of the Great Water the golden cock crows to rouse the sun's daughter, that she may spin the silver thread — the rays of the rising sun — for the day's weaving.
summary.zh: 偉大之水畔，金雞啼鳴以喚日之女，使其紡出銀線——即朝陽之芒——以織這一日。

passages.text: As for the sun's daughter, the golden cock crows on the edge of the Great Water — the Daugawa — to rouse her that she may spin the silver thread, that is, the rays of the rising sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

passages.text: Her chief task is to wash her golden jug — the solar disk — at evening; her morning task is the spinning of the silver thread on the golden wheel. Between cockcrow and sundown the daughter of the sun keeps the sky's household running: the cock, the spinner, and the washer are the three servants of the light, and the dainas give each his hour.

title.en: Little John Breaks the Golden Jug

region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

texts.period: Dainas recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: When, in other dainas, the solar jug is broken by 'little John', it is the waning strength of the sun's rays after Midsummer Eve — St. John's night — that the song is telling: the feast that breaks the sun's vessel also begins the year's turning.
summary.zh: 其他達伊納中，日之金壺為『小約翰』所碎——此乃詠仲夏夜（聖約翰之夜）後日光之衰；打破太陽之壺的節日，亦正是歲序轉折之始。

passages.text: When, in other dainas, the solar jug is broken by 'little John', the song is telling the waning strength of the sun's rays after Midsummer Night's Eve — St. John's Eve, June 23. The longest day breaks the vessel of the light; from the morning after the feast the year declines.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Midsummer festival of the Baltic — with its fires, its oak-wreaths, and its fern-seed hunts — stands exactly on the hinge: the night when the golden jug breaks is the night when the greatest bonfires are lit to help the sun. John the Baptist keeps the festival in the Christian calendar, and 'little John' the breaker of jugs keeps it in the dainas — one saint, one season, two names for the same turning.

title.en: The Sun Who Watches the Wheat: 'Many Are My Gifts in Sooth'
title.zh: 守望麥田的太陽：『吾賜甚豐』

region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於里加）

texts.period: Daina recorded 19th c. (Mannhardt); recorded by Gray 1918

source.work: L. H. Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V

summary.en: Asked where she delays so long, the Sun — daughter of God — answers that beyond the sea she watches the wheat and shepherds: 'Many are my gifts in sooth'; Morning Star makes her fire and Evening Star prepares her couch, and 'many are my kin in sooth.'
summary.zh: 問其為何久留，太陽——神之女——答：海之外她守望麥田與牧人：『吾賜甚豐』；晨星為其生火，晚星為其鋪榻——『吾親甚眾』。

passages.text: 'O thou Sun, daughter of God, where delayest thou so long, since thou hast from us withdrawn?' — 'O'er the sea, beyond the hills, wheat there is that I must watch, shepherds, too, that I must guard; many are my gifts in sooth.' 'Tending thee at morn and eve, who doth make for thee thy fire, who prepares thy couch for thee?' — 'Morning Star and Evening Star: Morning Star doth make my fire, Evening Star prepares my couch; many are my kin in sooth.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the daina as rendered by Gray, Baltic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part V; not verbatim.

passages.text: The little song sets out the whole Baltic theology of the harvest in eight lines: the sun is God's own daughter, sent to watch the wheat and the shepherds beyond the sea — the under-world of the west where the year's riches ripen — and her gifts are counted as the household's wealth. The Baltic farmer's year begins and ends with the Sun's own account-keeping: she watches what she gives.
